📌 Governance Quorum: Why a Vote Can Fail Even With a Majority

Main Points
⏺ Quorum is the minimum participation required for a decision to pass
⏺ Even if most voters choose “yes,” a proposal can fail without enough turnout
⏺ This post explains why DAOs need participation, not just votes

1️⃣ Core Idea — quorum protects a protocol from decisions made by a tiny group.
2️⃣ Example — if only a few wallets vote, the result may be technically “yes” but weakly representative.
3️⃣ Why It Matters — important changes should pass with meaningful participation from holders or delegates.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — quorum that is too high can freeze decisions, while quorum that is too low makes governance vulnerable.
5️⃣ Practical Check — when judging a DAO, review quorum rules, vote distribution, and delegate activity.

Final Thoughts

Governance is not only about who won. It also matters how many people showed up. Without quorum, a majority can be too small to count.

Here's a small fact about Python 🐍

The := operator is called the "walrus" because the symbols resemble the eyes and tusks of a walrus 🦭

It was introduced in Python 3.8 and allows you to assign a value to a variable and use it directly within the expression at the same time.

For example:

while (line := input("Say something: ")) != "quit":
    print(f"You said: {line}")

Without it, you would have to retrieve the value separately using input(), and then check it.

Have you ever used the := operator in your code?

Real Volume, Real Fees (Not "Farm Token" Emissions)

The Real Gold Rush: Expanding the Surface

The current volume is impressive, but here’s what’s truly exciting: the bottleneck isn't the demand from traders; it's the surface area available for the arbitrage engine to work across.

A few dozen pools can only capture a few dozen tokens' worth of flow. Imagine this same efficient arbitrage engine running across hundreds of pools that simply don't exist yet.

The traders are ready. The volume is real. The arbitrage engine is already running. What's missing is the liquidity to serve that volume and capture those fees across a much broader range of pairs.

Jordanian Management, Israeli Panic

Avigdor Liberman proposed that Jordan take administrative and security responsibility for Areas A and B of the West Bank. Netanyahu heard “Jordanian army.” 

The old Jordanian Legion was suddenly back in Israeli politics, this time through a podcast microphone.

Liberman said the Palestinian Authority had gone bankrupt and Israel needed another authority to administer Palestinian population centers. 

“We have to reach an understanding with the Jordanians, that they will manage Areas A and B, take security and administrative responsibility,” he said. 

His party later said he misspoke during the interview, saying Areas B and C when he meant A and B.

The correction does not alter the proposal. Liberman wants Israel to create territorial contiguity across Area C and retain “absolute control” there, while Jordan administers Areas A and B as part of what he calls an Israeli-Jordanian confederation. 

Israel keeps control of the territory linking its settlements. Jordan would administer the Palestinian cities and towns. The Palestinian Authority would lose the role it was created to perform.

Netanyahu told Liberman to retract the idea immediately: “I never believed that today you would propose that the Jordanian army control parts of the Land of Israel.” 

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said Liberman wanted to return Israel to the days of the Jordanian Legion. Itamar Ben-Gvir said Judea and Samaria were not “a parcel to be shipped to Jordan.” Shas leader Aryeh Deri said Liberman had forgotten what it meant to be right-wing. Former general Ofer Winter wrote: “Avet,” Liberman’s nickname, “you got confused.”

The blandest response came from Liberman’s own party. Yisrael Beytenu MK Yulia Malinovsky said: “We are not dealing with this at all.”

They are dealing with it. Liberman wants Jordan to govern Palestinians in territory Israel intends to dominate. Netanyahu’s coalition objects because saying that plainly would spoil the sovereignty campaign.

Bitcoin price fell toward $75,500 after the U.S. Senate rejected the CLARITY Act, while bearish momentum and nearby liquidation clusters raised the risk of another decline before the Federal Reserve’s rate decision.

❗️ The procedural vote ended 49-50, leaving the proposed crypto market structure legislation 11 votes short of the 60 required to move forward. The setback weighed on digital assets and U.S.-listed crypto companies as traders reassessed the outlook for federal market rules. Derivatives amplified the initial decline. Approximately $771 million in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, including about $568 million in long positions, according to market data cited after the vote. The imbalance showed that traders positioned for higher prices were caught by Bitcoin’s move below $76,000.

🔗 BTC also briefly fell through the lower Bollinger Band, which stood near $75,244, before returning inside the indicator. A move outside the lower band can signal heavy selling, but re-entry alone does not confirm that the correction has ended. The 4-hour relative strength index stood at 37.23, below its signal average of 45.70. RSI remains above the conventional oversold boundary of 30, leaving room for further weakness if buyers fail to defend the $75,000 region.
